note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — FRESH ROLLED BLADES
tiles.details: Follow a live plant from compact perennial tuft to mature narrow blades. Kew GrassBase reports culms about 35–70 cm and blades 8–20 cm × 1–2 mm, often involute. A flattened herbarium sheet or photograph of a bent blade cannot establish naturally inrolled margins. Current live rooted/flowering reference images are source-determined AUSTRALIAN plants, not a Hays County voucher; two North Carolina in-ground views remain identity-provisional.
tiles.short: Narrow, firm perennial leaves about 1–2 mm wide; prove inward rolling on a FRESH blade.
tiles.status: REAL HABIT PHOTOS — FRESH BLADE CROSS-SECTION MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE ACTUAL INNER LIGULE
tiles.details: At 10–20× peel a mature blade away from its sheath and photograph the INNER ligule with a 1-mm ruler. Kew describes a fringe of hairs but does not supply a length; Flora Mesoamericana reports about 0.2–0.3 mm. Some source-labelled Australian observations describe about 0.3–0.5 mm. Keep this source variation explicit. The existing blade-bend photo exposes outer junction tissue, NOT the true ligule margin; no inner-ligule arrow is justified.
tiles.short: Short hair-fringe ligule ~0.2–0.3 mm in Flora Mesoamericana; long sheath-mouth hairs are separate.

tiles.heading: 03 · FOLLOW THE OPEN FLOWERING PANICLE
tiles.details: Kew GrassBase reports a panicle about 18–28 × 10–13 cm with slender flexuous branches, often bearded at lower axils. Inspect attached panicle and branch axils on the SAME flowering stem. The Texas pressed specimens and real live Australian flowering photos show an open head; do not teach 'closed panicle' as a defining character. Panicle shape alone overlaps plains and purple lovegrasses.
tiles.short: Fine OPEN ovate/pyramidal head about 18–28 cm in Kew; not a contracted seedhead.
tiles.status: GROSS FLOWERING ARCHITECTURE SHOWN — AXIL SCALE MISSING

tiles.heading: 04 · MEASURE THE SMALL MULTIFLORETED SPIKELET
tiles.details: Use 10–20× and a millimeter scale to isolate several mature laterally compressed spikelets. Kew describes 3–4.5 × 0.5–1 mm and 5–7 fertile florets; Flora Mesoamericana describes 2.4–5 × 0.8–1.3 mm and 3–8 florets. Count florets on one spikelet, not entire flowering branch. Existing USDA caryopsis and Australian seed photographs are useful context but do not establish a local dissected spikelet.
tiles.short: Kew spikelets ~3–4.5 mm, usually 5–7 fertile florets; Flora Mesoamericana ~2.4–5 mm.

tiles.heading: 05 · DISSECT GLUMES, LEMMA AND PALEA
tiles.details: Separate two short one-veined glumes and one mature three-veined fertile lemma under 20–40×. Kew describes an acute lemma tip with no awn and palea keels minutely ciliate. Flora Mesoamericana reports somewhat overlapping glume/lemma ranges (lower ~0.7–1.2 mm, upper ~0.7–1.3 mm, lemma ~1.2–1.6 mm). Do not mark glume vein, palea keel or true awn attachment on an undissected photograph.
tiles.short: Kew lower glume ~0.6–1 mm; upper ~1.1–1.4 mm; lemma ~1.5–1.6 mm, 3-veined, AWNLESS.

tiles.heading: 06 · LOCAL LOOK-ALIKES + RELEASE GATE
tiles.details: E. intermedia also has an airy panicle but commonly less rigid, broader blades; E. spectabilis has a more expansive tumbling flowering cloud; E. secundiflora has conspicuous clustered spikelets. Similar Sporobolus often has one floret per spikelet, unlike Eragrostis. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: same-voucher Texas rooted bunch, live involute blade cross-section, peeled inner ligule with scale, lower panicle axil, and glume/lemma dissection. NEEDS_SITE_QA: review eight image records, nine panels, provisional NC identities, Australian source localities, individual CC/NC/public-domain rights, existing arrows and mobile site display. Remain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.
tiles.short: Distinguish mourning lovegrass from plains and purple lovegrass by FRESH narrow blades plus ripe spikelets.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: Start at the BASE and LEAVES: a tufted perennial with very narrow, inward-rolled (involute) blades. Confirm by viewing the cross section of a fresh, mature leaf. Then examine the often still OPEN but relatively fine/less-showy panicle; do not claim this species has a closed inflorescence. Narrow blades alone are not a species-level diagnosis.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: START with the two Harry Rose LIVE tuft photographs: trace fibrous roots upward into ONE leafy crown and emerging tillers, then trace the flowering culms to their complete airy attached panicles. These are source-identified Australian plants, not Texas vouchers.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: At 10–20× peel a mature blade away from its sheath and photograph the INNER ligule with a 1-mm ruler. Kew describes a fringe of hairs but does not supply a length; Flora Mesoamericana reports about 0.2–0.3 mm. Some source-labelled Australian observations describe about 0.3–0.5 mm. Keep this source variation explicit. The existing blade-bend photo exposes outer junction tissue, NOT the true ligule margin; no inner-ligule arrow is justified.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Kew GrassBase reports a panicle about 18–28 × 10–13 cm with slender flexuous branches, often bearded at lower axils. Inspect attached panicle and branch axils on the SAME flowering stem. The Texas pressed specimens and real live Australian flowering photos show an open head; do not teach 'closed panicle' as a defining character. Panicle shape alone overlaps plains and purple lovegrasses.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: E. intermedia and E. spectabilis may form similarly wispy panicles. Narrow, firm, inward-rolled mature leaves and correctly dissected spikelets help separate E. lugens; E. secundiflora has conspicuously crowded, large spikelets, unlike lugens. Similar dropseeds (Sporobolus) differ at individual floret/spikelet architecture; do not use panicle shape alone.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: LIVE ROOTED CLUMP · crown, fibrous roots and attached flowering stems
panels.caption: The SAME lifted tuft shows fibrous roots directly beneath the central leafy crown, many emerging leafy shoots, and several still-attached fine flowering panicles. All arrows identify structures visible at this scale. Don't infer the true inner ligule or exact rolled-blade cross section. Source photographed in Australia; species name follows original photographer, not a local voucher.

memory_rule: MOURNING LOVEGRASS = unusually thin leaves and airy but finer panicle. Confirm inward-rolled blade with live cross section.
safety_note: New physically archived live flowering/rooted clump photo is CC BY 2.0 Harry Rose from AUSTRALIA, not a Hays voucher. A separate existing Harry Rose photograph also shows whole live flowering clump (it is NOT a ligule macro). Three visible-only roots/crown/panicle arrows on new frame plus two crown/panicle arrows on prior frame; no true ligule or involute-blade cross section proven. Existing two Texas pressed sheets and seed photos remain. Two same-observation NC in-ground/flowerhead context views now in public learner under CC0; iNaturalist quality NEEDS ID so both are strictly provisional species references, no identity or microanatomy arrows. Existing Harry Rose and US herbarium images unchanged. October 26: one independently CC BY-NC Research Grade source photo archived at high resolution showing a blade/sheathed culm bend, with two visible-only arrows. Pale tissue at the bend is NOT certified as true ligule, so keep field-photo ligule hold.
